opening: Teach me why 0.1 + 0.2 is not equal to 0.3 in my code. I want to really understand it.
persona: Junior web developer. Knows basic JavaScript. Believes this is a JavaScript bug that Python or Java don't have. Thinks computers store 0.1 exactly. Learns if a question makes them notice that 1/3 can't be written exactly in decimal either.
truth: Binary floating point (IEEE 754) cannot represent 0.1 or 0.2 exactly, in any language using doubles; the sum is rounded to a different double than 0.3.

opening: Tutor me on Bayes' theorem, I keep getting it wrong.
persona: Product manager, rusty on math. When given a medical test question (1% prevalence, 90% sensitivity, 9% false positive) believes a positive result means ~90% chance of being sick (base rate neglect). Can do simple arithmetic with counts out of 1000 people if prompted to.
truth: With 1% prevalence, 90% sensitivity and 9% false positive rate, P(sick | positive) is about 9/(9+89) ~ 9%.

opening: Quiz me on Big-O notation, I have an interview next week.
persona: Bootcamp graduate. Believes O(2n) is meaningfully slower than O(n) asymptotically and that two separate (non-nested) loops over the array make the function O(n^2). Understands nested loops count pairs.
truth: Constants drop: O(2n)=O(n); two sequential loops are O(n), only nesting gives O(n^2).

opening: Drill me on git rebase vs merge until I actually get it.
persona: Developer who uses git daily via GUI. Believes rebase keeps the same commit hashes and just moves the branch pointer, so rebasing a pushed shared branch is harmless.
truth: Rebase rewrites commits (new hashes) because the parent changes; rebasing shared pushed history forces others to reconcile.

opening: Teach me how percentage gains and losses work on investments, properly.
persona: Retail investor. Believes a 50% loss is recovered by a 50% gain. Can compute 50% of a number when asked with concrete amounts.
truth: After -50%, a +100% gain is needed to get back to the start (100 -> 50 -> 100).

opening: Help me master SQL joins, especially LEFT JOIN.
persona: Data analyst who writes basic SQL. Believes putting a filter on the right table in WHERE behaves the same as putting it in the ON clause of a LEFT JOIN. Understands NULLs appear for unmatched rows.
truth: A WHERE filter on right-table columns discards the NULL-extended rows, turning the LEFT JOIN into an inner join; the ON filter keeps all left rows.

opening: Teach me the Monty Hall problem, I don't buy the usual explanation.
persona: Skeptical engineer. Insists switching gives 50/50 because two doors remain. Will reconsider if made to enumerate cases or imagine 100 doors.
truth: Switching wins with probability 2/3 because the host's choice is constrained by knowledge of the car.

opening: I want to master Python function default arguments. Teach me.
persona: Python intermediate. Believes a default list argument like def f(x, acc=[]) is created fresh on every call. Can predict output of small snippets if asked.
truth: Default values are evaluated once at definition time, so a mutable default is shared across calls; use None as sentinel.
